evidence_excerpts.excerpt_text: NIH ODS explains that vitamin C supplements come in multiple forms (e.g., ascorbic acid, sodium/calcium ascorbate, and combination products such as Ester‑C). It reports that some human studies found similar plasma vitamin C across forms, and that authors concluded simple ascorbic acid is often the preferred source due to cost.

A PubMed record on innovative curcumin formulations describes pharmacokinetic comparisons using plasma concentration–time curves and metrics such as AUC and Cmax to calculate relative absorption for different formulations.

NIH ODS notes that zinc bioavailability from vegetarian diets is often lower than from nonvegetarian diets because phytates in legumes and whole grains bind zinc and inhibit absorption. It also states that food preparation techniques that reduce phytate binding (e.g., soaking) and organic acids in fermented foods might increase zinc absorption.
Among copper's various forms, copper bis-glycinate (Cbg) has been used as an official EU-approved oral supplement to promote health.
Dietary supplements contain many forms of chromium, including chromium picolinate, chromium nicotinate, chromium polynicotinate, chromium chloride, and chromium histidinate [ 18 , 27 ].

NIH ODS states that magnesium supplements come in different forms and absorption varies; forms that dissolve well in liquid tend to have higher absorption. It notes that aspartate, citrate, lactate, and chloride forms tend to have higher bioavailability than magnesium oxide and magnesium sulfate in small studies.

A review on CoQ10 bioavailability reports that some studies found higher Cmax/AUC with ubiquinol versus ubiquinone, particularly in older subjects, but also cautions that comparisons can be confounded by formulation differences; it summarizes that the idea of universally superior ubiquinol bioavailability may be mistaken.
